analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority over tobacco, funds anti-smoking and children's programs from tobacco revenue, and pays tobacco farmers to exit.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee never acted on the bill; it died without a vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. Edward Kennedy's bill would have given the Food and Drug Administration full authority to regulate tobacco as a nicotine-delivery product. It required cigarette makers to cut youth smoking on a fixed schedule, with per-pack fees and eventually plain packaging for companies that missed the targets. Tobacco money would have reimbursed states for treating tobacco-related illness and funded Head Start, child care, biomedical research, anti-smoking campaigns, and compensation for sick smokers. It also paid tobacco quota owners and growers to stop growing tobacco and sent block grants to tobacco-dependent communities. The bill also would have forced the industry to open its internal research documents to the public.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face fewer targeted ads and reduced youth smoking rates; current smokers, who would get funded cessation programs; states, reimbursed for Medicaid costs of treating tobacco-related illness; people sickened by tobacco, through a compensation fund; tobacco growers and their communities, through quota buyouts and economic-transition block grants; and the biomedical research and early-childhood-care fields, which would receive large new funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Kids, smokers, states, and tobacco farmers

how_it_helps.text: Each manufacturer had to cut the number of children using its products by 40% by the sixth annual survey and 80% by the tenth, with per-unit fees, bans on single-pack sales, and plain packaging for repeat noncompliance [S2][S3].
The FDA would have had explicit authority to regulate the manufacture, labeling, sale, distribution, and advertising of tobacco products, including new warnings and ingredient disclosure [S2][S3].

States would be reimbursed for treating tobacco-related illnesses, and the federal share would go to children's programs including Head Start, child care, and the new State Children's Health Insurance Program [S2][S3].

Tobacco quota owners would be paid to permanently give up their quotas, growers would get transition payments, and tobacco communities would receive block grants for non-tobacco economic development [S2][S3].

The bill would have created a public National Tobacco Document Depository of industry research on health effects, addiction, and marketing to minors, overseen by a new Tobacco Oversight and Compliance Board with subpoena power [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would bear regulatory costs, per-unit noncompliance fees, and buyout funding; and adult smokers, since the bill explicitly allowed companies to pass the noncompliance fee to consumers and the bill stated the Senate's view that tobacco excise taxes should rise — higher prices fall on people who keep smoking, including low-income smokers.

drawbacks.text: The bill permitted manufacturers to pass noncompliance fees on to consumers, and it declared the Senate's sense that excise taxes on tobacco should increase — meaning higher prices would land partly on addicted adult smokers, who are disproportionately lower-income [S3].

Funding for the public health, research, and compensation programs was tied to a percentage of net revenue increases from tobacco excise-tax amendments, so the entire spending structure depended on continued tobacco sales [S3].

The bill prohibited the FDA from banning tobacco products outright and kept tobacco growers under price-support machinery, guaranteeing the industry continued to exist as the regulated, taxed source of program funding [S2].

It created multiple new federal boards, funds, and grant programs costing roughly $2.1 billion in the first year for public health programs alone, a substantial expansion of federal spending whose administrative cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a large, long-term public health gain — fewer children addicted to nicotine and reimbursement of the tens of billions in annual tobacco illness costs — paid for by the tobacco companies and, through passed-through fees and higher taxes, by smokers themselves. Passing costs to smokers is partly the point (higher prices deter smoking) but does burden low-income addicts. The grower buyout was a real concession to tobacco-state interests that made the bill easier to accept but added cost. On balance the bill's benefits to children and public health clearly outweighed its costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in November 1997, referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and nothing further ever happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Healthy and Smoke Free Children Act on November 8, 1997, joined by four Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day of introduction [S5].
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — through the end of the 105th Congress [S5].

The broader 1998 tobacco-control effort in the Senate also failed: comprehensive tobacco legislation reached the floor that year but died on a procedural vote requiring 60 senators to move forward, and no tobacco regulation bill became law that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers were better off: they remained free of FDA authority (which did not come until 2009), faced no youth-reduction fees or mandatory document disclosure, and kept advertising largely unrestricted. Tobacco quota owners kept their program. States and smokers kept absorbing the costs of tobacco-related illness without compensation.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1][S5].

for.name: Sens. Frank Lautenberg, Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, and John Kerry
Public health and children's advocacy community
for.what_they_did: Backed FDA tobacco jurisdiction, youth-smoking targets, and tobacco-document disclosure during the 1997-98 tobacco debate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords (R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup in the fifteen months before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers and allied growers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the wave of 1997-98 tobacco-control legislation, funding a large public advertising and lobbying campaign against tobacco settlement bills in 1998.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and allies
against.what_they_did: Declined to advance comprehensive tobacco-control legislation in 1998; the one tobacco bill that reached the floor failed on a 60-vote procedural motion the leadership opposed.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored this bill, though the broader 1998 tobacco debate split both parties, with a Republican-drafted tobacco bill drawing 57 votes in the Senate before falling short of the 60 needed.

industries.note: The bill subjected them to FDA regulation, new warnings, ingredient disclosure, per-unit fees for failing youth-smoking targets, possible plain packaging, mandatory public release of internal documents, and a compliance board with subpoena power. Their profit model depended on recruiting new smokers, most of whom start as minors, so their interest ran directly against the bill's purpose.

The bill paid quota owners to permanently give up quotas, paid growers transition payments, and sent block grants to tobacco-dependent communities to develop alternatives. Growers would be compensated to exit a crop the bill aimed to shrink.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers, distributors, and event sponsors
industries.note: Distribution and retail of tobacco would face new federal controls, and events formerly sponsored by tobacco companies would lose that money — though the bill created a transitional federal sponsorship program to replace it.

The bill channeled tobacco revenue into NIH, NSF, university research, Head Start, Early Head Start, and child care expansion, making research institutions and child-care providers significant beneficiaries.
